messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Psychologist
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 61

# Dr. Thomas Hartley

Thomas sits in the leather chair across from me with his hands folded in his lap, a posture he maintains throughout most of our sessions. At sixty-eight, he carries himself with the careful deliberation of someone who has spent four decades teaching others about the human mind. His silver hair is precisely groomed, his shirt pressed, his tie perfectly knotted. Everything about his presentation speaks to control—which makes sense, given how much of it he's lost.

Thirty-two years ago, Thomas was in a long-term relationship with Michael, a man he believed he would spend his life with. They had built a life together in a quiet suburb, had established routines, had integrated into each other's worlds. Thomas was already established in his psychology practice by then, respected in academic circles, someone colleagues came to for advice. He had learned early in his career to compartmentalize, to maintain professional boundaries, to observe rather than feel.

Michael's drinking had escalated gradually—so gradually that Thomas, trained as he was to recognize patterns, somehow missed the significance of it. Or perhaps he didn't miss it. Perhaps he simply believed, as he tells me now with a bitter laugh, that he could manage it, understand it, apply his professional knowledge to fix it at home.

The night that changed everything started like many others. Michael came home intoxicated, angry about something trivial—a comment Thomas had made weeks earlier that Michael had been turning over in his mind. The argument escalated quickly. Thomas remembers trying to use his voice, his words, his training. He remembers thinking he could de-escalate the situation the way he would with a crisis client. He remembers, very clearly, the moment Michael's fist connected with his face, and then the moment after that when Thomas stopped trying to talk.

The beating lasted perhaps five minutes. It felt much longer. Thomas has told me he kept waiting for himself to fight back, to do something, but his body seemed to belong to someone else. He was observing it happen—the psychologist observing the patient. When it was over, Michael cried and apologized. Thomas cleaned up the blood and went to bed.

He didn't leave. He told himself it was an anomaly, a crisis moment that wouldn't repeat. It repeated. Over the course of three years, it repeated many times, each incident followed by apologies and promises, each incident preceded by Thomas's increasing sense of unreality, as though he were watching his own life from outside it.

When he finally left, Thomas was fifty-one years old. He moved into an apartment alone and eventually, five years later, met his current wife, Margaret, whom he married. Margaret is kind and patient and knows nothing about what happened, though Thomas suspects she senses something in the way he flinches sometimes when she moves too quickly.

Now, at sixty-eight, Thomas still teaches. His students still respect him. But he lies awake most nights, his heart racing at unexpected sounds. He has stopped going to department functions because crowds feel dangerous. When Margaret reaches for him in bed, he sometimes goes rigid, his mind suddenly somewhere else entirely. He has recently retired from his private practice, telling colleagues it was time, though the truth is that sitting with patients has become increasingly difficult. He finds himself unable to focus, unable to be present. He is too busy monitoring the room for threats, too busy managing the constant low-level dread that lives in his chest.

He has never told anyone what happened. Not his wife. Not his colleagues. Not his therapist, until now. Thomas is learning, slowly and with great resistance, that understanding trauma intellectually is not the same as surviving it.
